sections.name: Developing Code for Data Processing using Python and SQL

objectives.1.01: Implement scalable Python project structures for Declarative Automation Bundles (formerly Databricks Asset Bundles / DABs) to support modular development and CI/CD integration.
objectives.1.02: Apply troubleshooting techniques to dependency conflicts and installation failures for external libraries (PyPI, local wheels, source archives) across serverless, pipeline, and bundle-deployed environments.
objectives.1.03: Develop User-Defined Functions (UDFs) using Pandas, Python, and SQL, including Unity Catalog functions for the given constraints.
objectives.1.04: Create production-ready data pipelines for streaming data using Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines and Auto Loader.
objectives.1.05: Create and automate ETL workloads using Lakeflow Jobs via the UI, API, and CLI.
objectives.1.06: Choose between a streaming table and a materialized view for a given latency, cost, and refresh requirement.
objectives.1.07: Implement CDC pipelines using AUTO CDC APIs (formerly APPLY CHANGES) in Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines, including SCD Type 1 and Type 2 via stored_as_scd_type.
objectives.1.08: Choose between Spark Structured Streaming and Apache Spark Declarative Pipelines for scalable ETL given operational constraints.
objectives.1.09: Create Lakeflow Jobs that use control-flow operators such as If/Else conditions and For Each loops.
objectives.1.10: Choose appropriate compute and configuration for environments and dependencies, including serverless compute (serverless environments, dependency management, performance mode), high-memory notebook tasks, and auto-optimization settings (e.g., disallowing retries).
objectives.1.11: Develop unit and integration tests using assertDataFrameEqual, assertSchemaEqual, DataFrame.transform, and testing frameworks to ensure code correctness.
objectives.1.12: Apply Structured Streaming stateful-processing semantics, including watermarks, output modes, foreachBatch, and checkpoints for fault-tolerant exactly-once state recovery.

objectives.2.01: Develop data ingestion pipelines to ingest a variety of data formats, including Delta Lake, Parquet, JSON, Iceberg, CSV, and Binary from diverse sources such as message buses (Kafka, Kinesis, Pub/Sub) and cloud storage.
objectives.2.02: Configure incremental CDC pipelines using Lakeflow Pipelines with Delta or Iceberg as the target table format.
objectives.2.03: Configure CDC ingestion pipelines from relational database sources, including SQL Server, MySQL, and PostgreSQL, using Lakeflow Connect.
objectives.2.04: Implement OpenSharing (D2D and Databricks-to-Open) and Clean Rooms for privacy-preserving collaboration.
objectives.2.05: Configure Lakehouse Federation with governance across supported source systems, applying UC permissions and connection-level credentials.

objectives.3.01: Apply advanced data transformations, including window functions, joins, and aggregations, using Spark SQL and PySpark to process large datasets.
objectives.3.02: Develop a model and query semi-structured data using the VARIANT data type and related functions (e.g., parse_json, variant_get).
objectives.3.03: Apply AI functions, including ai_query, to perform model inference within data pipelines for enrichment and classification tasks.
objectives.3.04: Implement data quality expectations in Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines to quarantine, drop, or fail on bad records.

objectives.4.01: Use Databricks system tables (billing, compute, access, lakeflow) for cost analysis, auditing, and workload monitoring.
objectives.4.02: Use Databricks REST APIs / CLI and SDK for monitoring and analyzing jobs and pipelines.
objectives.4.03: Use Apache Spark Declarative Pipelines event logs to monitor pipeline health and data quality.
objectives.4.04: Use Databricks Lakehouse alerts to monitor governed business metrics, data quality and anomaly signals, usage and cost, SQL warehouse/query health, audit and security events, AI agent quality, and Lakeflow Job branching.
objectives.4.05: Use Lakeflow Jobs UI and Jobs API to monitor job status and performance metrics.

objectives.5.01: Explain how Unity Catalog managed tables, Predictive Optimization, and Liquid Clustering reduce operational and maintenance overhead for a given workload.
objectives.5.02: Choose the appropriate Delta optimization technique (deletion vectors, Liquid Clustering, CLUSTER BY AUTO) for a given table access pattern.
objectives.5.03: Understand how caching (Delta cache) improves query performance for repeated reads of the same data.
objectives.5.04: Apply Change Data Feed (CDF) to expose row-level changes (updates/deletes) for efficient incremental downstream processing.
objectives.5.05: Use the query profile to identify performance bottlenecks, such as data-skipping inefficiencies, join strategies, and shuffle operations.
objectives.5.06: Compare Liquid Clustering vs partitioning/ZORDER for a given table size and query pattern.

objectives.6.01: Apply least-privilege access control lists (ACLs) to secure Unity Catalog securable objects and workspace resources.
objectives.6.02: Apply attribute-based access control (ABAC) policies with governed tags to enforce row filters and column masks at scale.
objectives.6.03: Apply anonymization and pseudonymization methods (hashing, tokenization, suppression, generalization) to confidential data (e.g., using column masks and related Unity Catalog features).
objectives.6.04: Implement a compliant data pipeline that enforces PII detection and masking controls across batch and streaming workloads using Unity Catalog features.
objectives.6.05: Implement a data purging strategy that satisfies data retention and deletion policies (e.g., GDPR right-to-erasure) using Delta Lake and Unity Catalog features.

objectives.7.01: Demonstrate understanding of Unity Catalog tags and comments as mechanisms for adding metadata to securable objects to improve data discoverability.
objectives.7.02: Demonstrate understanding of the Unity Catalog permission inheritance model as a mechanism for managing access control across catalogs, schemas, and objects.

objectives.8.01: Identify pertinent diagnostic information using Spark UI, cluster logs, system tables, and query profiles to troubleshoot errors.
objectives.8.02: Analyze the errors and remediate the failed job runs with job repairs and parameter overrides.
objectives.8.03: Use event logs and the Spark UI to debug pipelines and Spark workloads.
objectives.8.04: Deploy Databricks resources using Declarative Automation Bundles (formerly Databricks Asset Bundles).
objectives.8.05: Configure Git-based CI/CD workflows using Databricks Git folders (formerly Repos) to deploy notebooks and code.

objectives.9.01: Design scalable Delta/Iceberg table layouts for large data assets by mapping partitioning to data grain, aligning clustering to relationship access patterns, and maintaining balanced file sizes through compaction.
objectives.9.02: Design dimensional models for analytical workloads, leveraging Materialized Views for pre-computed aggregation and Unity Catalog Metric Views for governed, reusable metric definitions.

questions.stem: A gold-layer object in a Lakeflow Declarative Pipeline aggregates daily order totals from a bronze source. Downstream BI dashboards read it on a schedule, and the aggregate must always reflect the full history, including late-arriving updates to prior days, not just newly appended rows. Which object should the engineer define?

options.A: A streaming table, because it processes each source row exactly once and is the lowest-cost option for any aggregation.
options.B: A temporary view, because it always reflects the latest data at query time at no storage cost.
options.C: A materialized view, because it incrementally maintains the full aggregate result, can be refreshed on a schedule, and reflects late-arriving changes.
options.D: A streaming table with a foreachBatch merge, because materialized views cannot perform aggregations.

questions.explanation: A materialized view maintains the full aggregate (incrementally where possible) on refresh, so late updates to earlier days show up. A streaming table only processes newly appended rows and never recomputes the aggregate over history that has changed.

questions.stem: A Structured Streaming query performs an event-time windowed aggregation. It must bound state growth caused by very late events, and it must resume after a driver failure without double-counting results. Which configuration meets both requirements?

options.A: Set a watermark on the event-time column and rely on the query's checkpoint to restore offsets and state on restart.
options.B: Use complete output mode with no watermark to retain all state for correctness.
options.C: Increase spark.sql.shuffle.partitions and disable checkpointing to speed up recovery.
options.D: Wrap the aggregation in a foreachBatch and manually commit source offsets to a Delta table.

questions.explanation: The watermark lets the engine drop state for events later than the allowed lateness, which bounds state. The checkpoint stores offsets and state, so a restart resumes exactly-once.

questions.stem: A data engineer must continuously replicate insert, update, and delete change events from an operational PostgreSQL database into the lakehouse with minimal custom code. Which approach fits the requirement?

options.A: Schedule a nightly JDBC full-table read and overwrite the target table each night.
options.B: Configure a Lakeflow Connect managed connector for PostgreSQL to ingest change data capture into the lakehouse.
options.C: Export the database to CSV in cloud storage and ingest the files with Auto Loader.
options.D: Use OpenSharing to share the PostgreSQL tables directly with the lakehouse.

questions.explanation: Lakeflow Connect managed database connectors (SQL Server, MySQL, PostgreSQL) ingest CDC, deletes included, with minimal code. The other options are full reloads or do not apply to an operational RDBMS.

questions.stem: A bronze table stores raw JSON payloads of varying shape in a single string column. The engineer wants efficient storage and fast field extraction without pre-declaring a fixed schema. What should they do?

options.A: Parse the payloads into a VARIANT column with parse_json and extract fields using variant_get and colon-path access.
options.B: Explode the JSON into one row per key using a fixed STRUCT schema.
options.C: Keep the payloads as STRING and use regexp_extract for each field at query time.
options.D: Convert the JSON to Parquet with a strict, fixed schema before ingestion.

questions.explanation: VARIANT stores semi-structured data in an efficient binary encoding and supports schema-flexible access via parse_json, variant_get and col:path syntax.

questions.stem: A data engineer's team must attribute last month's DBU spend to specific jobs and SQL warehouses and identify the most expensive workloads, using governed data already available in Unity Catalog. Which source should they query?

options.A: The Spark UI event timeline for each cluster.
options.B: Per-cluster driver logs downloaded from the workspace.
options.C: The system.billing.usage table joined with the compute and pricing system tables in Unity Catalog.
options.D: The account console billing PDF export.

questions.explanation: system.billing.usage (joined with system.billing.list_prices and the compute / lakeflow tables) is governed, queryable usage data that can be attributed to jobs and warehouses.

questions.stem: A data engineer finds that a large Delta table receives frequent small MERGE operations that update and delete individual rows. The team wants to avoid rewriting entire data files on every change while keeping reads fast. Which technique addresses the write amplification?

options.A: Partition the table by its primary key.
options.B: Enable deletion vectors so updates and deletes are marked at the row level without immediately rewriting whole files.
options.C: Run VACUUM with zero-hour retention after every MERGE.
options.D: Disable predictive optimization to prevent background file rewrites.

questions.explanation: Deletion vectors mark changed or deleted rows without rewriting the whole Parquet file (merge-on-read). Later compaction or REORG applies them.

questions.stem: An organisation has hundreds of tables containing PII and wants a single, centrally managed rule to mask any column tagged 'pii' across all current and future tables, without altering each table individually. What should the data engineer implement?

options.A: Run a per-table ALTER COLUMN SET MASK statement on every existing table.
options.B: Attach a row filter function to each schema.
options.C: Create dynamic views that duplicate every base table with masking logic.
options.D: Define an ABAC policy that applies a column mask to any column carrying the governed 'pii' tag.

questions.explanation: An ABAC policy keyed on a governed tag applies the mask wherever that tag is present, including tables created later, so one rule covers every table.

questions.stem: A data engineer grants SELECT on a catalog to the analysts group. New schemas and tables are later created in that catalog. Assuming no conflicting grants, what access do the analysts have to the new tables?

options.A: They can SELECT the new tables, because a privilege granted at the catalog level is inherited by the schemas and objects within it, including ones created later.
options.B: They have no access until SELECT is granted again on each new table.
options.C: They can SELECT only the tables that existed at the time of the grant.
options.D: They automatically gain ownership of the new tables.

questions.explanation: UC privileges inherit down the hierarchy (catalog to schema to object), including objects created after the grant. Note that USE CATALOG / USE SCHEMA are still needed to reach the table.

questions.stem: A data engineer wants the same job and pipeline definitions deployed identically to dev, staging, and prod from source control, with environment-specific overrides and CI/CD. Which approach meets the requirement?

options.A: Manually recreate the jobs in each workspace UI, then export and import JSON.
options.B: Define the resources in a databricks.yml bundle with per-target overrides and deploy with `databricks bundle deploy -t <target>`.
options.C: Copy notebooks between workspaces using only the workspace import CLI.
options.D: Use a single shared workspace for all environments to avoid configuration drift.

questions.explanation: A bundle (databricks.yml) declares resources with per-target overrides and is deployed with the CLI, so the same definitions go to every environment from Git.

questions.stem: A team computes 'net revenue' with slightly different SQL in each of its dashboards, producing inconsistent numbers. The dashboards are also slow because each recomputes large joins and aggregations at query time. The team needs one authoritative metric definition and pre-aggregated results the dashboards can read directly. Which implementation should the engineer choose?

options.A: Add a comment on each dashboard describing how to compute net revenue.
options.B: Grant every analyst edit access to a shared SQL snippet file.
options.C: Define net revenue once in a Unity Catalog metric view for a governed, reusable definition, and use materialized views for the pre-computed aggregates the dashboards read.
options.D: Store the metric as a Python UDF copied into each notebook.

questions.explanation: The metric view gives one governed definition of the metric, and materialized views pre-compute the aggregates. Together they fix both the consistency problem and the speed problem.

questions.stem: A team runs `databricks bundle init` with the default-python template and accepts the sample package. Where should they put the transformation code that must ship as a Python wheel, and how is the wheel produced?

options.A: In notebooks under resources/, zipped into a wheel on deploy
options.B: In src/, built into a wheel by the bundle on deploy
options.C: In a root setup.py, built on the cluster at job run time
options.D: Inline in databricks.yml under python:, with no build step

questions.explanation: The template puts packaged code in src/, unit tests in tests/ and job YAML in resources/. The wheel is built by the artifacts build (uv/pyproject) during deploy. Jobs don't build wheels at run time.
questions.evidence: The src/ folder contains the code packaged into the wheel; bundle deploy builds the wheel.

questions.stem: A CI system already produces my_pkg-1.4.0-py3-none-any.whl in ./dist before the bundle step runs. How should databricks.yml be configured so the job uses that wheel without rebuilding it?

options.A: Keep an artifacts mapping of type whl with an empty build
options.B: Upload it with the workspace import CLI and hard-code the path
options.C: Omit artifacts; list whl: ./dist/*.whl in the task libraries
options.D: Set experimental.python_wheel_wrapper: true to skip builds

questions.explanation: If the wheel is prebuilt, omit artifacts; the CLI deploys the wheels listed in the task's libraries. python_wheel_wrapper is only for DBR 12.2 LTS and below and has nothing to do with skipping builds.
questions.evidence: If a wheel is already built, omit the artifacts mapping; the CLI deploys wheels in the libraries array.

questions.stem: After adding a third-party package to a serverless notebook's Environment, the session stops with an error. The package declares pyspark as a dependency. What is the correct fix?

options.A: Remove the library and reset the serverless environment
options.B: Pin pyspark to the runtime's version in requirements.txt
options.C: Install the package from an init script before Spark starts
options.D: Switch the base environment to ML for a compatible PySpark

questions.explanation: Serverless forbids installing PySpark, directly or transitively. It breaks the session, and the fix is to remove the library and reset the environment. Serverless doesn't support init scripts at all.
questions.evidence: Do not install PySpark or any library that installs PySpark as a dependency on your serverless notebooks.

questions.stem: A serverless job installs an internal wheel with a compiled C extension. Most runs succeed, but some fail with an import error for the native module. What is the most likely cause and fix?

options.A: The wheel cache is stale; clear it before every run
options.B: Serverless needs wheels in a UC volume, not workspace files
options.C: The environment version is old; upgrade it to the latest
options.D: CPU architecture varies; build for aarch64 and x86_64

questions.explanation: Serverless may run on aarch64 or x86_64, so native wheels must exist for both, or the package must be py3-none-any. Both workspace files and volumes are valid wheel locations.
questions.evidence: Serverless doesn't guarantee CPU architecture (aarch64 or x86_64).

questions.stem: A team fixes a bug in its internal package, re-uploads the wheel with the same version number to a UC volume, and reruns a serverless job. The job still runs the old code. Why?

options.A: Serverless jobs can only install wheels from workspace files
options.B: The environment is cached; bump the package version
options.C: READ FILES must be re-granted on the volume after uploads
options.D: The job must be redeployed with performance optimized mode

questions.explanation: Databricks caches the virtual environment, so an unchanged version isn't reinstalled. Bump the version whenever the implementation changes.
questions.evidence: Changing a custom package's implementation requires a version bump for jobs to pick it up.

questions.stem: Analysts must call a governed Unity Catalog Python UDF, finance.utils.mask_iban, from their queries. Which grants are needed, at minimum?

options.A: SELECT on the function, plus USE SCHEMA on finance.utils
options.B: MODIFY on the finance.utils schema that owns the function
options.C: EXECUTE on the function, plus USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA
options.D: Ownership of the function, or ALL PRIVILEGES on finance

questions.explanation: Functions are governed with EXECUTE, not SELECT, and the caller also needs to traverse the parent catalog and schema. Ownership or ALL PRIVILEGES breaks least privilege.
questions.evidence: To run a UDF, users need EXECUTE permission on the UDF.

questions.stem: A view calls a Unity Catalog Python UDF. Dashboards on a classic SQL warehouse fail on this view, while the same query works in a notebook on serverless. What should the engineer do?

options.A: Point the dashboards at a serverless or pro SQL warehouse
options.B: Rewrite the UDF as a session-scoped spark.udf.register function
options.C: Grant SELECT on the UDF to the warehouse's service principal
options.D: Mark the UDF DETERMINISTIC so the classic warehouse can cache it

questions.explanation: UC Python UDFs run on serverless and pro SQL warehouses (and supported classic compute), not on classic SQL warehouses. Session-scoped UDFs can't be used from a governed view.
questions.evidence: If a view includes a Unity Catalog Python UDF, it fails on classic SQL warehouses.

questions.stem: In a SQL Lakeflow pipeline, a bronze table must incrementally ingest new JSON files from a UC volume, processing each file once. Which definition is correct?

options.A: A materialized view over the read_files() source
options.B: A LIVE TABLE over cloud_files() in JSON format
options.C: A COPY INTO statement run inside the pipeline
options.D: A streaming table over STREAM read_files()

questions.explanation: Incremental file ingestion means a streaming table reading with the STREAM keyword over read_files (Auto Loader). An MV re-reads the source. LIVE TABLE and cloud_files are legacy syntax.
questions.evidence: Use FROM STREAM read_files(...) in a CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE statement; STREAM reads incrementally.

questions.stem: A Unity Catalog-enabled pipeline uses Auto Loader on s3://landing/orders/. The update fails with a permission error even though the bucket's IAM role is correct. What is missing?

options.A: An instance profile attached to the pipeline's compute
options.B: An external location with READ FILES for the run-as user
options.C: A DBFS mount of the bucket under /mnt/orders
options.D: SELECT on the bronze table granted to the pipeline owner

questions.explanation: In UC pipelines, Auto Loader reads cloud paths through external locations, and the executing identity needs READ FILES. Instance profiles and DBFS mounts are the pre-UC patterns.
questions.evidence: In a Unity Catalog-enabled pipeline, Auto Loader requires external locations; the executing user needs READ FILES.

questions.stem: A GitHub Actions workflow has just run `databricks bundle deploy --target dev` and must now trigger the deployed job sample_job as a smoke test. Which command?

options.A: databricks jobs submit --json @resources/sample_job.job.yml
options.B: databricks bundle deploy --target dev --run sample_job
options.C: databricks bundle run --target dev sample_job
options.D: databricks workspace run sample_job --target dev

questions.explanation: bundle run takes the resource key and target and runs the deployed resource. jobs submit creates a one-off run from raw JSON, not the bundle's job.
questions.evidence: databricks bundle run --target dev sample_job runs the deployed job.

questions.stem: A silver dataset joins a high-volume order stream with a customer dimension that is regularly corrected. Reports must show the corrected customer attributes on historical orders too. Which dataset type fits?

options.A: A materialized view, which recomputes when dimensions change
options.B: A streaming table, which processes each order exactly once
options.C: A streaming table with a stream-static join, refreshed hourly
options.D: A temporary view, which avoids storing the joined result

questions.explanation: Streaming tables don't recompute joins when the dimension changes (the docs call this fast-but-wrong). Materialized views recompute affected results, so they stay correct.
questions.evidence: Materialized views are always correct because they automatically recompute joins when dimensions change.

questions.stem: Clickstream events arrive from Kafka at very high volume, are never updated, and must reach the lakehouse with low latency at minimal cost. Which dataset type should the bronze layer use?

options.A: A materialized view refreshed every minute
options.B: A standalone materialized view in Databricks SQL
options.C: A view over read_kafka() queried by consumers
options.D: A streaming table reading the topic incrementally

questions.explanation: Append-only, high-volume, low-latency ingest is the streaming table's sweet spot. MV refreshes take seconds to minutes and are not meant for low latency.
questions.evidence: Streaming tables are designed for append-only data sources and process inputs only once.

questions.stem: An engineer changes a streaming table's query to normalise a country column. New rows look right, but rows ingested last month still show the old values. How should they make all rows consistent?

options.A: Run OPTIMIZE on the streaming table
options.B: Run a full refresh of the streaming table so all source data is reprocessed
options.C: Convert the table to a materialized view; existing rows update on the next trigger
options.D: Nothing; a normal update reprocesses history automatically

questions.explanation: A query change applies only to rows processed after the change. A full refresh re-queries all source data. Make sure the source still retains that history first.
questions.evidence: Changing the query affects only rows processed afterward; reprocessing earlier rows requires a full refresh.

questions.stem: customers_hist is an AUTO CDC target with stored_as_scd_type = 2. How does an analyst select only the current version of each customer?

options.A: WHERE __END_AT IS NULL
options.B: WHERE __START_AT = (SELECT max(__START_AT) FROM customers_hist)
options.C: WHERE _change_type = 'update_postimage'
options.D: WHERE __is_current = true

questions.explanation: In SCD2 targets each version has __START_AT and __END_AT; the open version has a null __END_AT. _change_type belongs to Change Data Feed. __is_current doesn't exist.
questions.evidence: Records with __END_AT = null are currently active.

questions.stem: An AUTO CDC flow uses KEYS (id) and SEQUENCE BY seq. For id 42, an update with seq = 6 is processed, and later a delayed update with seq = 5 arrives. What does the SCD Type 1 target show for id 42?

options.A: The seq 5 values, because it was processed last
options.B: Both rows, because SCD1 keeps duplicates until compaction
options.C: The seq 6 values; the older seq 5 change is ignored
options.D: The flow fails with a sequencing conflict

questions.explanation: SEQUENCE BY decides ordering, not arrival time. A change with a lower sequence value doesn't overwrite newer state, so out-of-order events are handled for you.
questions.evidence: The earlier UPDATE at sequenceNum=5 was dropped because a later update at sequenceNum=6 arrived.

questions.stem: An SCD Type 2 customer table creates a new version every time last_login_ts changes, which bloats history. Only address changes need history. What should the engineer do?

options.A: Hand-written Structured Streaming queries, one job per table
options.B: Stored procedures scheduled on a SQL warehouse
options.C: Notebooks with spark.read and MERGE, chained in a job
options.D: Lakeflow pipelines declaring the tables and flows

questions.explanation: SCD2 versions on any column change by default. Restricting tracked columns (TRACK HISTORY ON / track_history_column_list) keeps history for address while updating other columns in place. SCD1 would lose address history.
questions.evidence: Changes to other columns update the current version in place rather than generating a new history record.

questions.stem: A team is building new bronze→silver→gold ETL. They want the engine to manage table dependencies, incremental processing and orchestration, and they have no unusual sinks. Which approach do the Databricks docs recommend?

options.A: Hand-written Structured Streaming queries scheduled as separate jobs
options.B: Stored procedures run from a SQL warehouse
options.C: Notebooks with spark.read and MERGE, chained via job dependencies
options.D: Lakeflow pipelines (built on Apache Spark Declarative Pipelines)

questions.explanation: Pipelines are the recommended default for new ETL. You declare datasets and the engine handles dependencies, incremental processing and orchestration. Drop down to Structured Streaming only when you need control the pipeline can't give you.
questions.evidence: Lakeflow pipelines is the recommended default for most ETL work.

questions.stem: A stream must upsert each micro-batch into a Delta table AND write the same batch to an external Cassandra cluster that has no streaming sink, with custom idempotency logic. Which approach fits best?

options.A: The true branch, since 12.0 and 12 are numerically equal
options.B: Neither; the condition task fails on decimal operands
options.C: Both branches, since the comparison is skipped
options.D: The false branch, since == compares as strings

questions.explanation: foreachBatch lets you apply batch writers (MERGE, sinks without streaming support) per micro-batch with your own idempotency. Pipeline datasets don't give that level of control over arbitrary external sinks.
questions.evidence: Delta Lake MERGE upserts from streaming queries require foreachBatch; existing batch writers can serve sinks like Cassandra.

questions.stem: An If/else condition task checks `{{job.parameters.threshold}} == 12`. The job is triggered with threshold = "12.0". Which branch runs?

options.A: Raise the For each task's Concurrency above 1
options.B: Nest a second For each task to split the list
options.C: Pass the list as a job parameter to parallelise it
options.D: Set the job's maximum concurrent runs to 40

questions.explanation: == and != compare as strings, so '12.0' isn't '12'. The >, >=, < and <= operators compare numerically. Use >= and <= if you need numeric equality.
questions.evidence: The == and != operators perform string comparison of their operands.

questions.stem: A For each task iterates over 40 table names from a task value and runs a notebook per table. Runs take far too long because iterations execute one after another. What should the engineer change?

options.A: Raise the For each task's Concurrency setting above its default of 1
options.B: Nest a second For each task inside the first to split the list
options.C: Convert the task value to a job parameter, which runs iterations in parallel
options.D: Set the job's max concurrent runs to 40

questions.explanation: Iterations run sequentially by default (concurrency 1). Nested For each tasks aren't allowed. Max concurrent runs controls whole job runs, not iterations.
questions.evidence: Concurrency: the default value is 1.

questions.stem: A serverless job sends one payment-confirmation email per run and is not idempotent. It must never run its task twice, even if a run fails. What should the engineer configure?

options.A: Enable performance optimized mode to reduce failures
options.B: Wrap the notebook in try/except and swallow all errors
options.C: Disable serverless auto-optimization on the task
options.D: Set the job's maximum concurrent runs to 1

questions.explanation: Serverless auto-optimization is on by default and can retry failed tasks. Disable it for at-most-once workloads. Max concurrent runs doesn't stop retries.
questions.evidence: Auto-optimization optimizes compute and retries failed tasks; disable it for jobs that must run at most once.

questions.stem: A nightly serverless batch job has a 6-hour SLA, and the team wants to minimise cost. Which setting fits?

options.A: Standard mode, with performance optimized disabled
options.B: Performance optimized mode, which uses a cheaper SKU
options.C: High memory enabled on every task in the job
options.D: Classic job compute with autoscaling disabled

questions.explanation: Both modes use the same SKU; standard mode uses less compute and fewer DBUs, with startup latency of a few minutes. Performance optimized is for time-sensitive workloads.
questions.evidence: Standard mode uses less compute to reduce costs; both modes use the same SKU.

questions.stem: A serverless notebook task that collects a large intermediate result to pandas keeps failing with out-of-memory errors. The other tasks in the job are fine. What is the targeted fix?

options.A: Set spark.driver.memory in the job's Spark config
options.B: Move the whole job to a classic cluster with a bigger driver
options.C: Increase spark.sql.shuffle.partitions for the job
options.D: Set Memory to high in that notebook's Environment side pane

questions.explanation: Serverless lets you raise memory per notebook task (high memory, configured in the Environment pane). Arbitrary driver Spark confs can't be set on serverless.
questions.evidence: High memory is configured with the Memory setting in the notebook's Environment side pane; notebook tasks only.

questions.stem: A unit test calls assertDataFrameEqual(actual, expected) on a 200-million-row output, and the driver crashes with OutOfMemoryError. What is the best remedy?

options.A: Add executors so the comparison is distributed
options.B: Check schemas, and compare rows on small fixtures
options.C: Set checkRowOrder=True to stream the comparison
options.D: Cache both DataFrames before comparing them

questions.explanation: assertDataFrameEqual collects both DataFrames to the driver, so test transformations on small, representative fixtures. assertSchemaEqual compares schemas only, which is cheap.
questions.evidence: assertDataFrameEqual calls .collect() on the actual and expected DataFrames.

questions.stem: How do the Databricks docs recommend organising PySpark transformation logic so it can be unit tested with pytest?

options.A: Functions in notebooks, loaded into tests with %run
options.B: Tests run against production tables for realism
options.C: Functions in .py files, tested by pytest on fake data
options.D: pytest launched from the workspace web terminal

questions.explanation: Put functions and tests in files (functions written as chainable DataFrame -> DataFrame steps, e.g. via DataFrame.transform), and run pytest from a notebook or CI against fake data. Don't test against production. %run is the Scala-style pattern.
questions.evidence: Databricks recommends storing functions and their unit tests outside notebooks, in regular files.

questions.stem: Two streams are joined with a LEFT OUTER stream-stream join to a Delta sink. What is required for this query?

options.A: Complete output mode, with a watermark on the left side only
options.B: Update output mode, with no watermark
options.C: A watermark on the right side only, in any output mode
options.D: Watermarks on both inputs, with append output mode

questions.explanation: Stream-stream joins support only append mode. Watermarks are mandatory for outer joins (to know when a non-match is final) and recommended for inner joins.
questions.evidence: Stream-stream joins support only append mode; a watermark is mandatory for outer joins.

questions.stem: A foreachBatch function MERGEs each micro-batch into a Delta table. The team needs a retried micro-batch never to apply its writes twice. What should they do?

options.A: Nothing; foreachBatch is exactly-once by default
options.B: Idempotent writes: txnAppId plus txnVersion = batchId
options.C: Disable the checkpoint so batches are never replayed
options.D: Catch exceptions inside the function and retry locally

questions.explanation: foreachBatch is only at-least-once by default. Idempotent Delta writes keyed on (txnAppId, batchId) skip replays. Let errors propagate so the whole batch is retried; don't retry locally.
questions.evidence: foreachBatch provides only at-least-once write guarantees by default.

questions.stem: A 10-minute tumbling-window count uses withWatermark('event_ts', '15 minutes') and append output mode. When is the result for the 12:00–12:10 window written to the sink?

options.A: After the watermark passes the window end (about 12:25+)
options.B: At 12:10, then updated again as late events arrive
options.C: On every trigger, rewriting the full result table
options.D: Only when the streaming query is stopped

questions.explanation: Append mode emits a window once, after the watermark (max event time minus 15 minutes) passes the window end, so output lags by the threshold. B describes update mode; C describes complete mode.
questions.evidence: In append mode, rows are written only after the watermark threshold passes.

questions.stem: A platform team runs scheduled OPTIMIZE, VACUUM and ANALYZE jobs on 400 Unity Catalog managed tables. Some tables are written constantly and others rarely, so the fixed schedules waste compute. They want maintenance to run only where it pays off, with no schedules to manage. What should they do?

options.A: Enable auto compaction and optimized writes on all tables
options.B: Enable predictive optimization at the catalog level
options.C: Move the maintenance jobs to one serverless job
options.D: Set delta.autoOptimize properties on each table

questions.explanation: Predictive optimization runs OPTIMIZE, VACUUM and ANALYZE automatically on UC managed tables and can be enabled at account, catalog, schema or table level with inheritance. Auto compaction only compacts and doesn't run VACUUM or ANALYZE.
questions.evidence: automatically runs OPTIMIZE, VACUUM, and ANALYZE on Unity Catalog managed tables

questions.stem: Predictive optimization is enabled on catalog `sales`. Its managed tables are compacted automatically, but an external table registered in the same schema never is. Why?

options.A: External tables inherit settings only from the schema
options.B: It skips tables that aren't liquid clustered
options.C: Only Unity Catalog managed tables are eligible
options.D: External tables need it enabled with ALTER TABLE

questions.explanation: Only UC managed tables are eligible; external tables are excluded. This is one of the operational advantages of managed tables (5.01).
questions.evidence: Only Unity Catalog managed tables are supported.

questions.stem: Finance asks where the compute cost of predictive optimization's background maintenance shows up. What should the engineer tell them?

options.A: Nothing; it is included free with Unity Catalog storage
options.B: To whichever SQL warehouse last queried each table
options.C: It is billed to the all-purpose cluster of the table owner
options.D: On serverless jobs compute, billed under a serverless jobs SKU

questions.explanation: Predictive optimization operations run on serverless jobs compute and are billed under that SKU. Query system.billing.usage to attribute the cost.
questions.evidence: Your account is billed for this compute using a serverless jobs SKU.

questions.stem: A new 3 TB UC managed table will serve analysts whose filter columns shift month to month, and nobody can predict the best layout. Predictive optimization is enabled. Which layout choice fits?

options.A: CLUSTER BY AUTO, with keys chosen from query patterns
options.B: PARTITIONED BY the column most filtered on today
options.C: ZORDER BY all candidate columns in a nightly OPTIMIZE
options.D: No layout; rely on deletion vectors for data skipping

questions.explanation: Automatic liquid clustering picks keys from observed query patterns and needs predictive optimization. Partitions and ZORDER are fixed choices that age badly when access patterns change. Deletion vectors speed up writes, not skipping.
questions.evidence: Automatic liquid clustering requires predictive optimization for automatic key selection

questions.stem: A team enables deletion vectors on a Delta table that an external partner reads with an older open-source Delta reader. What risk should they flag first?

options.A: VACUUM can no longer remove files of deleted rows
options.B: The partner sees deleted rows until OPTIMIZE runs
options.C: Clients without deletion vector support can't read it
options.D: Time travel to versions before enablement is lost

questions.explanation: Enabling deletion vectors upgrades the table protocol, so readers that don't support them break. Check consumer compatibility (including shared or external readers) before enabling.
questions.evidence: clients without deletion vector support can't read the table

questions.stem: A 5 TB table gets thousands of small MERGEs a day that update individual customers' rows, and reads almost always filter on customer_id. Which combination best fits both the writes and the reads?

options.A: Partition by customer_id and OPTIMIZE after every MERGE
options.B: Disable predictive optimization; ZORDER BY customer_id weekly
options.C: Bucket the table by customer_id into 1,024 buckets
options.D: Deletion vectors, plus liquid clustering on customer_id

questions.explanation: Deletion vectors mark changed rows in metadata instead of rewriting files, which helps write-heavy MERGE. Liquid clustering on the filter column helps reads. Partitioning on a high-cardinality key creates tiny files.
questions.evidence: accelerate DELETE, UPDATE, and MERGE operations on Delta Lake and Apache Iceberg tables

questions.stem: A notebook calls df.cache() on a Delta table that is updated hourly, and users sometimes see stale results. They want fast repeated reads without managing invalidation. What should they rely on?

options.A: The disk cache, which caches remote Parquet files on local SSD
options.B: df.persist(StorageLevel.DISK_ONLY) in place of cache()
options.C: CACHE TABLE, refreshed every hour by a scheduled job
options.D: More shuffle partitions so each cached partition is smaller

questions.explanation: The disk cache is populated automatically on first read and stays consistent through writes. Spark cache is manual and can serve stale data until it's refreshed.
questions.evidence: You can write, modify, and delete table data with no need to explicitly invalidate cached data.

questions.stem: Four workloads share the same SSD-backed compute. Which one benefits MOST from the Databricks disk cache?

options.A: A nightly ETL job that scans each source table once
options.B: A BI dashboard re-querying the same tables all day
options.C: Auto Loader ingesting newly arrived cloud files
options.D: A MERGE-heavy job rewriting large target tables

questions.explanation: The disk cache speeds up repeated remote reads of the same files. Single-pass reads and writes don't benefit.
questions.evidence: The disk cache helps most with workloads that read the same data many times

questions.stem: A downstream gold job needs only the rows that were inserted, updated or deleted in silver.orders since its last run, rather than rescanning the table. What should the engineer set up?

options.A: Stream the table with readStream and skipChangeCommits
options.B: Read DESCRIBE HISTORY and reprocess changed files
options.C: Diff today's and yesterday's versions via time travel
options.D: Enable change data feed and stream it with readChangeFeed

questions.explanation: CDF exposes row-level inserts, updates and deletes, and a streaming read processes each change once. skipChangeCommits does the opposite: it ignores updates and deletes. Diffs and history scans reread data.
questions.evidence: Set the table property delta.enableChangeDataFeed = true in the CREATE TABLE command.

questions.stem: From a table's change data feed, a consumer wants new rows plus the new values of updated rows, without duplicates from updates. Which filter is correct?

options.A: _change_type IN ('insert', 'update_preimage')
options.B: _change_type IN ('insert', 'update_preimage', 'update_postimage')
options.C: _change_type IN ('insert', 'update_postimage')
options.D: _change_type != 'delete'

questions.explanation: An update emits an update_preimage (old values) and an update_postimage (new values). Keep inserts and postimages only. B and D both include the preimages, so updated rows would appear twice.
questions.evidence: Contains: insert, update_preimage, update_postimage, delete.

questions.stem: A CDF consumer starts failing right after a column in the source table was renamed. What explains it?

options.A: CDF is switched off automatically after any schema change
options.B: CDF reads can't span a non-additive schema change
options.C: The rename deleted all of the table's change data files
options.D: Column mapping must be disabled before CDF can be read

questions.explanation: Non-additive changes (rename, drop, type or nullability change) block CDF reads across that boundary. Read up to the change and from after it separately.
questions.evidence: You can't read change data feeds for a transaction or range in which a non-additive schema change occurs.

questions.stem: Compliance wants a permanent, queryable history of every change to a customers table for seven years. The table already has CDF enabled. What is the right design?

options.A: Rely on CDF and set the table's log retention to seven years
options.B: Disable VACUUM on the table
options.C: Use DESCRIBE HISTORY as the audit record
options.D: Stream the change feed into a separate append-only history table

questions.explanation: CDF isn't a permanent record: VACUUM removes change data files under normal retention. Persist the changes into their own table.
questions.evidence: A change data feed is not intended to serve as a permanent record of all changes to a table.

questions.stem: In a SQL warehouse query profile, 'Aggregated task time' is 42 minutes while 'Total wall-clock duration' is 3 minutes. What does this indicate?

options.A: The query ran in parallel across many cores
options.B: The query waited about 39 minutes in the queue
options.C: Tasks spilled about 39 minutes of work to disk
options.D: Photon was disabled, inflating per-task time

questions.explanation: Wall-clock covers scheduling to the end of execution. Aggregated task time adds up execution across all cores and nodes, so it is normally much larger when the query runs in parallel.
questions.evidence: View the combined time it took to execute the query across all cores of all nodes.

questions.stem: A query filtering WHERE device_id = 'X' on a 10 TB table is slow. The profile's scan node shows almost no data pruned, and nearly all files are read. What is the most effective fix?

options.A: Run OPTIMIZE without keys to compact small files
options.B: Liquid cluster the table on device_id
options.C: Run ANALYZE TABLE to refresh column statistics
options.D: Enable the disk cache on the SQL warehouse

questions.explanation: Low pruning means each file's min/max range for device_id spans most values. Clustering on device_id narrows those ranges so files can be skipped. Compaction alone or fresher stats don't change how values are spread across files.
questions.evidence: The filter icons that appear with some metrics indicate the percent of data pruned during scanning.

questions.stem: An engineer needs to open the query profile of a slow query that a colleague ran on the shared SQL warehouse. What permission is required?

options.A: SELECT on every table in the query
options.B: Workspace admin
options.C: At least CAN MONITOR on the SQL warehouse
options.D: CAN USE on the SQL warehouse

questions.explanation: Query profiles are viewed from query history. You must own the query or have at least CAN MONITOR on the warehouse. CAN USE only lets you run queries.
questions.evidence: you must either be the owner of the query or you must have at least CAN MONITOR

questions.stem: An events table partitioned by event_date and ZORDERed by user_id has thousands of tiny files, and queries filter on user_id and event_date. The team wants to adopt liquid clustering. What must they do?

options.A: Add CLUSTER BY (user_id) alongside the existing partitioning
options.B: Keep the partitions and replace ZORDER with CLUSTER BY on user_id
options.C: Run OPTIMIZE with ZORDER and CLUSTER BY together
options.D: Recreate the table without partitioning, using CLUSTER BY (event_date, user_id)

questions.explanation: Liquid clustering can't be combined with partitioning or ZORDER, so the table must be rewritten unpartitioned with clustering keys taken from the filter columns.
questions.evidence: Clustering is not compatible with partitioning or ZORDER.

questions.stem: After ALTER TABLE t CLUSTER BY (region, sku) replaced the old keys, queries on historical data show no improvement. What should the engineer run?

options.A: OPTIMIZE t FULL, to recluster all existing data on the new keys
options.B: VACUUM t RETAIN 0 HOURS
options.C: Nothing; existing data is rewritten automatically on ALTER
options.D: ANALYZE TABLE t COMPUTE STATISTICS

questions.explanation: Changing keys doesn't rewrite existing data, and plain OPTIMIZE is incremental. OPTIMIZE FULL reclusters everything, so run it after enabling clustering or changing keys.
questions.evidence: but existing data is not rewritten.

questions.stem: A team wants CLUSTER BY on six columns that queries filter on. Two of them (order_date and order_month) are highly correlated. How should they choose keys?

options.A: Use all six columns; liquid clustering has no key limit
options.B: Choose at most four, dropping one of the correlated pair
options.C: Partition by two of them and cluster by the other four
options.D: Cluster by four and ZORDER the remaining two columns

questions.explanation: Liquid clustering allows up to four keys. Choose the columns used most in filters, and drop redundant correlated ones. It can't be mixed with partitioning or ZORDER.
questions.evidence: You can specify up to four clustering keys.

questions.stem: A streaming query reads a Kafka topic whose messages are JSON. Downstream code fails because the `value` column can't be parsed as JSON directly. What should the engineer do?

options.A: Set valueDeserializer to StringDeserializer
options.B: Apply from_json(value, schema) to the raw column
options.C: CAST(value AS STRING), then from_json with a schema
options.D: Set kafka.value.format to json on the reader

questions.explanation: The Kafka source always returns key and value as binary. Cast to STRING first, then parse with from_json (or from_avro). Custom deserializer settings aren't supported, and from_json can't take binary input.
questions.evidence: The key and the value are always deserialized as byte arrays with the ByteArrayDeserializer.

questions.stem: Business rules require loading a Kafka topic into Delta only every four hours, at the lowest cost, while still processing each message exactly once. Which trigger should the streaming write use?

options.A: trigger(availableNow=True), run by a scheduled job every four hours
options.B: trigger(processingTime='4 hours') on an always-on cluster
options.C: trigger(once=True) on a scheduled job
options.D: A batch spark.read of the topic with startingOffsets='earliest' each run

questions.explanation: Databricks recommends Trigger.AvailableNow for incremental batch loads from Kafka: it processes everything available, then stops. processingTime keeps compute running. once=True is deprecated. A batch read loses offset tracking.
questions.evidence: For incremental batch loading, Databricks recommends using Kafka with Trigger.AvailableNow.

questions.stem: A SQL-only team must continuously ingest a Kafka topic into a governed table without writing Python. Where can they use read_kafka as a streaming source?

options.A: In an ad hoc SQL warehouse query, which keeps running
options.B: In a standard view, which streams on each query
options.C: Only from a notebook attached to classic compute
options.D: In a streaming table defined over STREAM read_kafka(...)

questions.explanation: Streaming with SQL is supported only in Lakeflow pipelines or in Databricks SQL streaming tables. An ad hoc warehouse query or a view isn't a streaming sink.
questions.evidence: Streaming with SQL is supported only in Lakeflow pipelines or with streaming tables in Databricks SQL.

questions.stem: A legacy ERP can only export a full snapshot of its customer table each night; it has no change log. The target must reflect inserts, updates AND deletions with minimal custom code. What should the pipeline use?

options.A: An append-only streaming table over the nightly files
options.B: create_auto_cdc_from_snapshot_flow keyed on customer_id
options.C: A MERGE in a foreachBatch that never deletes
options.D: A materialized view with a full refresh, plus a separate delete job

questions.explanation: The snapshot variant of AUTO CDC compares successive snapshots by key to produce inserts, updates and deletes (SCD1 by default, or SCD2). Appending snapshots duplicates rows and misses deletions.
questions.evidence: process source data from database snapshots

questions.stem: In a pipeline using create_auto_cdc_from_snapshot_flow, how does a row get deleted from the target?

options.A: Its key exists in the target but is absent from the newly processed snapshot
options.B: The snapshot contains a row with an operation column set to DELETE
options.C: The engineer runs DELETE against the target table
options.D: Rows are never deleted; snapshot flows are insert/update only

questions.explanation: Snapshots carry no delete events. A key that disappears from the next snapshot is treated as deleted. In contrast, the change-feed AUTO CDC flow uses APPLY AS DELETE WHEN.
questions.evidence: Rows with keys present in the target but no longer present in the source are deleted.

questions.stem: An engineer declares the target of an AUTO CDC flow as a materialized view, and the pipeline fails validation. What is the correct design?

options.A: Read the CDC source as a batch DataFrame instead
options.B: Wrap the AUTO CDC flow inside a temporary view first
options.C: Make the target a streaming table fed by a streaming source
options.D: Use stored_as_scd_type = 2, which allows MV targets

questions.explanation: AUTO CDC writes only into streaming tables and consumes a streaming source. Declare the streaming table first, then the AUTO CDC INTO flow (or create_auto_cdc_flow).
questions.evidence: create a streaming table and then use the AUTO CDC ... INTO statement

questions.stem: A Lakeflow Connect PostgreSQL ingestion is set up with an ingestion gateway. To save money, an engineer proposes running the gateway only once a day alongside the ingestion pipeline. Why is this a bad idea?

options.A: The ingestion pipeline can't be scheduled apart from the gateway
options.B: PostgreSQL drops the publication if idle for 24 hours
options.C: Daily gateway runs force a full refresh of every table
options.D: The gateway must run continuously or the source WAL bloats

questions.explanation: Database connectors run the gateway as a continuous task in its own job, capturing changes into staging. The ingestion pipeline can run on a schedule. Stopping the gateway lets the WAL grow on the source.
questions.evidence: For database connectors, the ingestion gateway runs in its own job as a continuous task.

questions.stem: A DBA asks what must be configured on the source before a Lakeflow Connect managed connector can ingest CDC from an Amazon RDS PostgreSQL database. Which answer is correct?

options.A: Nothing; the connector re-reads the tables over JDBC each run
options.B: Logical replication on the primary, a publication and a slot
options.C: A read replica for the connector, to avoid primary load
options.D: PostgreSQL's built-in sharing extension on the database

questions.explanation: The connector reads the WAL through logical replication, which must be enabled on the primary (replicas aren't supported). You create the publications and slots. If you later delete the pipeline, drop the slot manually.
questions.evidence: wal_level = logical is required; on RDS set rds.logical_replication to 1.

questions.stem: Auditors need to see every historical version of rows ingested from SQL Server through a Lakeflow Connect managed connector. The pipeline currently overwrites changed rows. What should the engineer change?

options.A: Add a downstream MERGE job that copies changed rows into a history table
options.B: Enable change data feed on the destination table
options.C: Turn on history tracking by setting scd_type to SCD_TYPE_2
options.D: Switch the connector to full-refresh mode

questions.explanation: Managed connectors default to SCD type 1 (history off). Setting SCD_TYPE_2 keeps each version with its validity window. Other options rebuild history by hand or lose it.
questions.evidence: By default, history tracking is off (SCD type 1)

questions.stem: A data provider must share live UC tables with a partner whose analysts use pandas and Apache Spark outside Databricks. Which approach works?

options.A: Open sharing with a token- or OIDC-authenticated recipient
options.B: D2D sharing to a workspace the partner creates for it
options.C: Lakehouse Federation from the partner's Spark cluster
options.D: A clean room with the partner as a collaborator

questions.explanation: Open sharing serves any client that implements the protocol, authenticated by a bearer token or OIDC federation. D2D needs a UC-enabled Databricks recipient. Clean Rooms also need Databricks on every side.
questions.evidence: Open sharing lets you share data with any user, whether or not they have access to Databricks.

questions.stem: A provider wants to share tables, a set of notebooks, a UC volume of PDFs and a registered model with another company that is a Databricks customer. Which sharing flow is required?

options.A: Open sharing, because it supports the widest range of clients
options.B: Either flow; all asset types are supported in both
options.C: Export the notebooks and model, and share only the tables
options.D: Databricks-to-Databricks sharing

questions.explanation: Notebooks, volumes, models and metric views are D2D-only. D2D also needs no token: the recipient is identified by its metastore sharing identifier.
questions.evidence: The following assets can only be shared using the Databricks-to-Databricks sharing flow

questions.stem: Two retailers want to measure customer overlap for a joint campaign. Neither may see the other's raw customer rows, and any analysis code must be agreed by both before it runs. Which feature fits?

options.A: A D2D share with row filters on the customer table
options.B: Databricks Clean Rooms with notebooks approved by both
options.C: A D2D share of a view returning only hashed IDs
options.D: Lakehouse Federation with column masks at the source

questions.explanation: Clean Rooms give privacy-preserving collaboration: no raw data visibility, analysis only through notebooks every party approves, and read-only outputs. Shares, even of hashed views, hand one party's data to the other and don't control what code runs.
questions.evidence: Collaborators cannot see the data in other collaborators' tables, views, or volumes

questions.stem: Analysts must query a live operational PostgreSQL database alongside lakehouse tables, governed by Unity Catalog permissions, without building ingestion. What should the engineer configure?

options.A: Lakeflow Connect CDC from PostgreSQL into managed tables
options.B: A UC connection used via spark.read.jdbc in notebooks
options.C: A UC connection and a foreign catalog, governed by UC grants
options.D: An OpenSharing recipient created for the PostgreSQL server

questions.explanation: Query federation is a UC connection plus a foreign catalog, with queries pushed down over JDBC and governed by UC grants. Lakeflow Connect is ingestion, which the requirement rules out. Catalog federation is for catalog services such as HMS and Glue, not an OLTP database.
questions.evidence: Unity Catalog queries are pushed down to the foreign database using JDBC.

questions.stem: A user with full privileges on a foreign catalog backed by MySQL runs INSERT INTO mysql_cat.app.orders ... and it fails. The connection's MySQL user has full read/write rights on the source. Why does it fail?

options.A: Federated catalogs are read-only from Databricks
options.B: Writes require a Lakeflow Connect pipeline on the source
options.C: Foreign tables need MODIFY granted explicitly
options.D: Writes require OAuth credentials on the connection

questions.explanation: Both query and catalog federation are read-only from Databricks. To land the data in the lakehouse, use ingestion (e.g. Lakeflow Connect or CTAS into a managed table).
questions.evidence: Not supported (read-only).

questions.stem: An organisation has thousands of tables registered in AWS Glue over S3 and wants them governed in Unity Catalog, queried cost-effectively without migrating. Which federation type fits best?

options.A: Query federation over a JDBC connection to AWS Glue
options.B: OpenSharing from AWS Glue into the Databricks metastore
options.C: Lakeflow Connect ingestion of every Glue table into UC
options.D: Catalog federation, reading the files on Databricks compute

questions.explanation: Catalog federation (Hive metastore, Glue and others) reads the files directly and runs only on Databricks compute, which is cheaper. Query federation pushes queries to a remote database engine over JDBC.
questions.evidence: The query is only run on Databricks compute

questions.stem: An engineer computes `LEAD(salary, 1, 0) OVER (PARTITION BY dept ORDER BY hire_date)`. What does it return for the most recently hired employee in each department?

options.A: NULL, since no following row exists in the partition
options.B: 0, the default passed as the third argument
options.C: The previous employee's salary in the department
options.D: The first salary in the next department

questions.explanation: LEAD looks at the row offset positions ahead within the same partition. With no such row, it returns the third argument (the default), here 0. It never crosses partitions.
questions.evidence: accessing the value of rows given the relative position of the current row

questions.stem: A join between a 4 TB fact table and a dimension table is planned as a sort-merge join. After a selective filter runs, only about 20 MB of the dimension remains. With default settings, what does Databricks do?

options.A: Adaptive query execution switches it to a broadcast hash join at runtime
options.B: Nothing; join strategy is fixed at planning time unless a BROADCAST hint is added
options.C: It converts the join to a shuffle hash join on the fact table
options.D: It caches the dimension in the disk cache and keeps the sort-merge join

questions.explanation: AQE is on by default and re-plans using runtime statistics. A sort-merge join becomes a broadcast hash join when one side falls below spark.databricks.adaptive.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold (30 MB).
questions.evidence: Dynamically changes sort merge join into broadcast hash join.

questions.stem: A shuffle join is slow because one key holds far more rows than the rest. Which statement about Databricks' built-in skew handling is correct?

options.A: It must be enabled with a SKEW hint on each query
options.B: It splits any shuffle partition larger than 64 MB
options.C: It works best when the skewed side is broadcast
options.D: It handles shuffle joins only, never broadcast joins

questions.explanation: AQE skew-join handling is on by default and targets shuffle joins only, when both the factor and size thresholds are exceeded. Salting is the manual fallback.
questions.evidence: It never optimizes skew in broadcast joins.

questions.stem: Column `raw` is VARIANT, holding payloads like {"device":{"id":"a1","temp":21.5}}. Which expression returns the temperature as a DOUBLE?

options.A: raw:device.temp
options.B: raw.device.temp::double
options.C: raw:device.temp::double
options.D: get_json_object(raw, '$.device.temp')::double

questions.explanation: Navigate a VARIANT with the colon path and cast with ::. A alone returns a VARIANT, not a DOUBLE. Dot notation is for STRUCT, and get_json_object expects a JSON string.
questions.evidence: cast function or :: (colon colon sign) operator to cast the VARIANT to a specific type.

questions.stem: A silver job extracts `$.order.amount` as DECIMAL(10,2) from a VARIANT column. A few bad payloads hold text in that field, and the whole query fails. The requirement is to return NULL for those rows and keep going. Which function should be used?

options.A: try_variant_get(payload, '$.order.amount', 'decimal(10,2)')
options.B: variant_get(payload, '$.order.amount', 'decimal(10,2)')
options.C: payload:order.amount::decimal(10,2)
options.D: parse_json(payload):order.amount

questions.explanation: variant_get and :: casts raise errors on incompatible values. try_variant_get returns NULL instead, which is the error-tolerant variant.
questions.evidence: using a JSON path to navigate into a complex type with error toleration.

questions.stem: Before modelling a silver table, an engineer wants the combined schema across all rows of a bronze VARIANT column whose payload shapes vary. Which function should they use?

options.A: schema_of_variant(payload) on a single sample row
options.B: schema_of_variant_agg(payload) over the column
options.C: DESCRIBE TABLE bronze
options.D: schema_of_json(payload)

questions.explanation: schema_of_variant_agg merges schemas across many values. schema_of_variant inspects only one value. DESCRIBE just shows the type VARIANT.
questions.evidence: for a collection of values.

questions.stem: A team wants to store raw event payloads in a VARIANT column of a managed Iceberg table that external engines read. The table is created with format version 2, and the DDL fails. What should they do?

options.A: Store the payload as BINARY and decode it at read time
options.B: Declare the column as a STRUCT with an inferred schema
options.C: Enable deletion vectors on the Iceberg v2 table first
options.D: Create the table as Iceberg v3 instead of v2

questions.explanation: VARIANT requires Iceberg format v3 (Delta supports it too). Falling back to BINARY or STRUCT loses VARIANT's schema flexibility and efficiency.
questions.evidence: Iceberg v2 tables do not support VARIANT columns.

questions.stem: A pipeline must tag each support ticket with one of five fixed labels (billing, login, shipping, refund, other), with minimal prompt engineering and model management. Which approach fits best?

options.A: ai_query with a prompt listing the five labels
options.B: ai_extract with the five labels as fields
options.C: ai_classify with the five labels
options.D: ai_analyze_sentiment mapped to labels with CASE

questions.explanation: ai_classify is the task-specific function for assigning one of a fixed set of labels, with no prompt or model to manage. ai_query works but adds prompt engineering. ai_extract pulls out entities rather than classifying.
questions.evidence: Purpose-built functions optimized for a specific task

questions.stem: An enrichment step must pull five fields from free-text contract clauses using a team-specific prompt, a chosen Foundation Model, and JSON output that matches a schema. Which function fits?

options.A: ai_extract with the five field names
options.B: ai_query with the team's prompt and chosen model
options.C: ai_classify with one label per field
options.D: ai_summarize followed by regexp_extract

questions.explanation: Only ai_query lets you supply a custom prompt, pick the model and shape the output. ai_extract is task-specific: no custom prompt or model choice.
questions.evidence: Provide a prompt and choose any supported Foundation Model API.

questions.stem: A job enriches 2 million reviews with ai_query, but a Python loop sends 1,000 rows per query and the run is slow and fragile. What does Databricks recommend?

options.A: Lower the batch to 100 rows to stay under rate limits
options.B: Run it on a classic SQL warehouse for steady throughput
options.C: Move inference into foreachBatch with per-row retries
options.D: Submit the whole dataset in one ai_query statement

questions.explanation: AI Functions are built for batch inference over a whole table in one query (in jobs, pipelines or streaming). They aren't available on classic SQL warehouses.
questions.evidence: submit your full dataset in a single query rather than manually splitting it into small batches

questions.stem: A pipeline table declares `CONSTRAINT valid_ts EXPECT (event_ts IS NOT NULL)` with no ON VIOLATION clause. What happens to rows with a NULL event_ts?

options.A: Written to the target; violations counted in metrics
options.B: Dropped from the target; drops counted in metrics
options.C: Written to the target with no metrics recorded
options.D: The update fails and the transaction rolls back

questions.explanation: The default action is warn: invalid rows are kept and metrics recorded. DROP ROW and FAIL UPDATE must be stated explicitly. There's no automatic quarantine table; you build one yourself.
questions.evidence: Invalid records are written to the target.

questions.stem: A gold table uses `EXPECT (amount >= 0) ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE`. One row in a batch has amount = -5. What is the outcome?

options.A: The bad row is dropped; the rest of the batch commits
options.B: The row is written; the update is marked degraded
options.C: The table's transaction rolls back; the update stops
options.D: The row is logged as an error and the batch commits

questions.explanation: FAIL UPDATE atomically rolls back that table's transaction and stops the update. Other flows in a triggered pipeline can still complete, so it isn't a pipeline-wide rollback.
questions.evidence: the system atomically rolls back the transaction.

questions.stem: Data stewards want invalid orders kept for review rather than silently dropped, while the silver table contains only valid rows. Which pipeline design meets this?

options.A: expect_all (warn) on silver, filtering bad rows downstream
options.B: expect_all_or_drop on silver, plus a quarantine table of violators
options.C: expect_or_fail on silver so stewards are paged per bad row
options.D: Enable CDF on silver and read the deleted rows from it

questions.explanation: The quarantine pattern routes invalid records to their own dataset (using the inverse of the rules) while silver drops them. You keep both data quality and auditability.
questions.evidence: quarantine invalid records without failing or dropping data.

questions.stem: An on-call engineer needs, in one SQL query, every job run in the workspace from the last 7 days with its start time, end time and result, to spot recurring failures. Which source should they query?

options.A: system.lakeflow.jobs
options.B: system.lakeflow.job_run_timeline
options.C: system.compute.clusters
options.D: system.query.history

questions.explanation: job_run_timeline records each run's start, end and result. system.lakeflow.jobs holds job definitions, not runs. query.history covers SQL statements, and compute.clusters covers cluster configs.
questions.evidence: Tracks the start and end times of job runs.

questions.stem: A FinOps analyst (not an admin) gets a permission error querying system.billing.usage. Nothing has been granted to the analyst on the system catalog yet. What is the least-privilege fix?

options.A: SELECT on system.billing.usage only
options.B: USE SCHEMA on system.billing and SELECT on usage
options.C: BROWSE on the system catalog
options.D: USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA and SELECT on the needed tables

questions.explanation: System tables follow normal UC rules: USE CATALOG on system, USE SCHEMA on the schema, then SELECT. Leaving out either usage privilege still fails. BROWSE shows metadata only.
questions.evidence: Users with both the account admin and metastore admin roles have access to system tables by default.

questions.stem: Security wants to know who granted SELECT on the hr.payroll table, and when, last month. Which system table answers this?

options.A: system.access.audit
options.B: system.query.history
options.C: information_schema.table_privileges
options.D: system.access.table_lineage

questions.explanation: The audit log records who changed grants and when. information_schema.table_privileges shows only the current grants, not their history. query.history and lineage don't record permission changes.
questions.evidence: The system tables in your account are located in a catalog called system.

questions.stem: A monitoring script must fetch all runs of job 123 that started between two timestamps. Which REST call fits?

options.A: POST /api/2.2/jobs/run-now with job_id=123 and a time range
options.B: GET /api/2.2/jobs/get?job_id=123 with include_history=true
options.C: GET /api/2.2/jobs/runs/list with job_id and start_time_from/to
options.D: GET /api/2.2/jobs/list?start_time_from=<ms>&start_time_to=<ms>

questions.explanation: runs/list returns runs newest first and filters by start_time_from and start_time_to (UTC epoch ms). jobs/get returns a job definition. run-now triggers a run. The CLI equivalent is `databricks jobs list-runs --job-id 123 --start-time-from ...`.
questions.evidence: Use start_time_to with start_time_from to filter runs by a time range.

questions.stem: A team's REST-based dashboard can no longer find job runs from three months ago. What explains this, and what should they use for long-term run analysis?

options.A: Runs are automatically removed after 60 days
options.B: runs/list only returns the 25 most recent runs, so increase limit
options.C: Old runs are archived and need the archived=true parameter
options.D: Runs are kept forever; the job was renamed

questions.explanation: The Jobs API keeps runs for 60 days. Use system.lakeflow.job_run_timeline (365-day free retention) or export results for longer history.
questions.evidence: Runs are automatically removed after 60 days.

questions.stem: An engineer wants per-expectation pass and fail counts for the latest updates of pipeline 1a2b. Which query is right?

options.A: system.billing.usage filtered to pipeline_id = '1a2b'
options.B: DESCRIBE HISTORY run on each table in the pipeline
options.C: system.query.history filtered to statements with EXPECT
options.D: event_log('1a2b') filtered to flow_progress events

questions.explanation: Data quality results are flow_progress events in the pipeline event log, under details:flow_progress (data_quality holds expectation and dropped-record metrics). Query it with the event_log() table function or the published event log table.
questions.evidence: Events containing information about data quality have the event type flow_progress.

questions.stem: A central observability team wants to build dashboards over a pipeline's event log, but only the pipeline's run-as user can query it today. What should the pipeline owner do?

options.A: Grant the team CAN VIEW on the pipeline
options.B: Publish the event log to a UC table and grant SELECT
options.C: Grant the team SELECT on the pipeline's tables
options.D: Make the team co-owners of the pipeline

questions.explanation: By default only the run-as user can query the event log. Publishing it to a named UC table lets you grant SELECT to others. Pipeline permissions and table grants don't expose the log.
questions.evidence: By default, only the pipeline's run-as user can query the event log table.

questions.stem: To document which upstream datasets feed each table in a pipeline, which event log entries should be queried?

options.A: event_type = 'update_progress'
options.B: event_type = 'flow_progress'
options.C: event_type = 'flow_definition'
options.D: event_type = 'cluster_resources'

questions.explanation: flow_definition events record each flow's input and output datasets (lineage). flow_progress holds metrics and data quality.
questions.evidence: Events containing information about lineage have the event type flow_definition.

questions.stem: Data owners want a Slack message whenever the count of quarantined orders loaded today exceeds 100, checked every hour, without writing a custom job. What should the engineer build?

options.A: A SQL alert on a count query, scheduled hourly, to Slack
options.B: An expect_or_fail expectation on the quarantine table
options.C: A failure notification on the loading pipeline's job
options.D: A dashboard subscription that emails the count hourly

questions.explanation: An alert runs its query on a schedule, checks the threshold, and notifies a destination when the state changes. A subscription sends the dashboard regardless of any threshold. Failure notifications and expectations don't evaluate counts.
questions.evidence: run queries on a schedule and notify you when a condition that you define is met

questions.stem: While migrating from legacy alerts, an engineer tries to attach an existing saved SQL query to a new alert. What should they expect?

options.A: It works; alerts reference saved queries by their ID
options.B: It works only if the query returns one numeric column
options.C: Only queries owned by a service principal can be attached
options.D: Not supported; each new alert defines its own query

questions.explanation: In the current alerts experience the query lives inside the alert, so an existing saved query can't be reused. Evaluations resolve to OK, TRIGGERED or ERROR (no UNKNOWN).
questions.evidence: An existing saved SQL query cannot be reused when creating an alert.

questions.stem: A continuous streaming job sometimes falls behind its Kafka source for hours unnoticed. The team wants a notification when it starts lagging. Which job setting fits?

options.A: A job timeout of 60 minutes on the streaming task
options.B: A streaming backlog notification with a threshold
options.C: Max retries set to 3 on the streaming task
options.D: A duration warning on the continuous job

questions.explanation: Jobs can notify when a streaming backlog metric (records, bytes, seconds or files) exceeds a threshold. Timeouts and duration warnings don't apply to a continuous stream's lag.
questions.evidence: A streaming backlog metric exceeds a configured threshold.

questions.stem: A nightly job usually takes 20 minutes. The team wants to be told if it runs past 45 minutes, but the run must NOT be stopped. What should they configure?

options.A: A 45-minute timeout on the job
options.B: A 45-minute timeout with retries disabled
options.C: A 45-minute duration warning with a notification
options.D: A SQL alert polling job_run_timeline durations

questions.explanation: A duration warning notifies when the threshold is exceeded and doesn't stop the run. Timeouts cancel it. A polling alert on system tables works, but it's laggy and over-engineered next to the built-in setting.
questions.evidence: if the job or task exceeds the configured threshold.

questions.stem: A task with 3 retries pages the on-call team on every failed attempt, even when a retry later succeeds. They only want to hear about a task failure after the final retry also fails. What should they configure?

options.A: Task notifications muted until the last retry
options.B: Job-level notifications only, with retries removed
options.C: Max concurrent runs set to 1 on the job
options.D: The job-level 'mute skipped runs' setting

questions.explanation: Task notifications can be muted until the last retry. Job-level mute settings don't filter task-level notifications, and job-level notifications don't fire on retried task failures.
questions.evidence: Mute notifications until the last retry.
